You have five days to explore the site and collect the most beautiful objects that are buried there. Will you be able to manage the team entrusted to you on a daily basis to optimize your excavations? Be smarter than the competition to emerge from Quetzal unscathed. At the beginning of each turn, roll your meeple dice and discover your team. Send your groups to different places in the city to collect the artifacts you are most interested in. Be careful, even if you arrive first your opponents can still steal your place! Build the best collection of artifacts and deliver them at the right time to earn improvements and victory points. At the end of the 5th round, whoever has the most points is the winner. Gameplay The game lasts for 5 rounds. At the beginning of each round, you'll roll your meeples, to determine who will be part of your team this round. Then, in turn order, players will place a group of meeple on an available spot on the board. Once every meeple as been placed, the board spots are resolved. Rolling the meeples At the beginning of each rounds, your meeples are rolled as if they were dice. The job that they will represent is determined by the face they land on: - black side means this meeple is now considered an adventurer - white side means this meeple is now an archeologist - on the side or standing means this meeple is considered wild and could be used as either adventurer or archeologist In addition to basic meeples, you also have a Character meeple. This meeple is rolled with the others, but is always considered wild. For any meeple that ends up standing, you receive 1 coin. Placing the meeples In turn order, players will choose one location on the board and send one or several meeples to that spot. This goes on until everyone has placed all their meeples. Locations all have a banner showing what meeples can be sent there, what the benefit is and what's the activation turn order: - locations usually accept only one type of meeple, either adventurers or archeologists: a white meeple means only archeologists can be sent there, a black one means only adventurers, a bicolor meeple means adventurers OR archeologists, and a grey meeple means adventurers AND/OR archeologists - some locations accept only one meeple, with an associated coin cost you must pay to sent a meeple there. - some locations use a bidding system. To send meeples there, you need to send more meeples than the previous player, the former meeples are returned to their player. - some locations accept any number of meeples, from different players If you send meeples to the Camp, it activates immediatly. You can send any meeple there, at no cost, allowing you to receive 1 coin and reroll on of your available meeples. If the meeple is standing, you receive an additional coin. Activating the locations Once every meeple has been placed, the locations are activated in the following order: 1 Stela of Knowledge Only 1 archeologist can be sent there, but you cannot use that spot if you are in possession of the first player marker Reward: 1 Discovery + First player marker Note: Discoveries allow you to advance on the discovery track, rewarding you with bonus at specific steps. 2 Temple The Temple has 5 spots, where only 1 archeologist can be sent at each spot, for a coin cost. The lowest spot can be occupied by either an archeologist or an adventurer. Reward: From top to bott

[Rating: 2/10] A mix of worker placement and set collection, with the added quirk of meeples that you literally 'roll' with the side they land on determining which spaces they can use (with some being set by the first person to place there in a manner slightly reminiscent of Keyflower). Overall I found it a bit forgettable and doubt I will be rushing to play it again.

[Rating: 2/10] An awful, awful game where the designers thought it would be 'unique' to have actions decided not by the roll of the dice, but by the roll of the Meeples. Yes, you read that right. The Meeples.   The rest of the game was an unimaginative worker placement *yawn* mistake of a game.

[Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  I suppose it is fine for a simple worker placement, set collection game with a gimmick. Not enough here for a return visit though. Colorful!

[Rating: 3/10] I love this meeple throwing thing, but it doesn't fit a game like that. Seems to be euro style game, being ridiculously random (eg. double reward for staying "in foot"...). Throwing meeples to bid with them - no, please... I wolud love to see a game with throwing meeples, but with rest of a game matching to this.

[Rating: 3/10] A nice mix of worker placement, bidding, set collection, and power ups. Oh, and rolling meeples, but that's so gimmicky. Unfortunately it was pretty one note without much to really drive things home.

[Rating: 4/10] I found it repetitive and boring.   Played it 3 players and I found the player interaction frustrating because it was almost absent except for the ship delivery where the biding/auction system makes it too competitive and unforgiving.   Mechanic-wise, it's not as bad as other games I'd give 4/10. But here it's also because of the lack of originality (an umpteenth worker placement game that doesn't do better than preceding ones) and the offensive choice of theme.

[Rating: 4/10] People are still releasing cookie-cutter worker placement games in 2020? Yeah, it has two kinds of workers, but most spaces accept either.  Also, people still do colonialist-imperialist theming like this in 2020?

[Rating: 4/10] Quetzal is a dressed up set collection game. You get to roll your meeples which is a fun little gimmick, but this does little to liven gameplay. The game is rather straightforward, with too many methods for gaining cards, and not enough motivation to sell them early. My plays have been dominated by a player who accumulates early and liquidates late. There is not incentive (aside for a potential meeple discount) to trade early. Its a bit too roundabout for a family game and has too low of a skill ceiling to appeal to core gamers, leaving in a sort of no man's land.

[Rating: 4/10] Played on BGA. It's dull. Mimics the auction style of Keyflower but everyone's meeple stash is public so there's no real tension. Also a player only ever has 7 meeples to bid with per round so bidding wars are limited.  Most of the action spaces are about acquiring artifacts, but the artifacts are all very similar. There's little joy in, for example, acquiring the clay pot vs acquiring the clay pot that also gives you a coin.  There are upgrade tiles but each player is limited to 2 at a time so no engine-building potential.  Arbitrarily the game ends after five rounds, but nothing changes from

[Rating: 4/10] Rolling the meeples to determine the types of workers you have available is a neat gimmick, but the rest of the game fell flat. The set collection has no tension, with so many opportunities to get and sell cards and the cards being too similar to make which ones you get not feel very important.
